prompt: Tap the finding that most changes immediate management.

roles.pivot: The finding that commits you to a different action.
roles.contributory: Right line of reasoning, but not decisive on its own.
roles.noise: Does not change what you do next.

clauses.text: A 62-year-old man has had crushing central chest pain for two hours, and has already been given sublingual GTN for the pain.
clauses.feedback: The GTN is the reflex almost any chest pain gets — reasonable right up until you know which heart chamber has actually failed.

clauses.text: His ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF.
clauses.feedback: Right line. This localises the infarct to the inferior territory, which is exactly where you should start thinking about right ventricular involvement. But an inferior STEMI on its own is still managed conventionally.

clauses.text: Pulse is 108 bpm and blood pressure is 84/52 mmHg.
clauses.feedback: Worth noticing, and it should raise your suspicion. But hypotension alone doesn't tell you whether the safe move is more fluid or less — pump failure from left heart congestion needs the opposite of what preload-dependent right heart failure needs.

clauses.text: His JVP is visible at the earlobe with him sitting upright.
clauses.feedback: Very close. A raised JVP tells you the right heart is under strain. But raised JVP with hypotension is also the picture of left ventricular failure with congestion, where you would offload rather than fill. One further finding separates those two.

clauses.text: His chest is completely clear on auscultation.
clauses.feedback: This is the finding that reverses your reflexes.

cases.resolution: Raised JVP with hypotension in an inferior STEMI could mean either right ventricular infarction (preload-dependent, needs filling) or left ventricular failure with congestion (needs offloading) — the two need opposite treatment. Clear lung fields are what settle it: they rule out the pulmonary congestion of LV failure, confirming the right ventricle is the failing chamber. Per ESC 2023 ACS guidance, RV infarction specifically requires aggressive IV fluid to maintain right heart output, and nitrates and other preload-reducing drugs — including the GTN already reached for on arrival — should be avoided, as they can precipitate abrupt, profound hypotension. The clear chest is what should make you stop the GTN and start the fluids, not the other way round.

clauses.text: A 24-year-old woman with known asthma has been wheezy and breathless since the morning.
clauses.feedback: Background. It tells you which illness you are in, not how severe this episode is.

clauses.text: She cannot complete a sentence in one breath.
clauses.feedback: A genuine severity marker — this is one of the features of acute severe asthma. But it puts her in a category that is still managed with maximal medical therapy on the ward.

clauses.text: Peak flow is 32% of her predicted best.
clauses.feedback: Again a real severity marker, and again it lands in 'acute severe'. Keep going — something here escalates her further.

clauses.text: Oxygen saturation is 94% on high-flow oxygen.
clauses.feedback: Falsely reassuring, and a common trap. Saturations are maintained by supplemental oxygen until very late in acute asthma. A number that looks acceptable is not evidence that she is safe.

clauses.text: Arterial blood gas shows a PaCO2 of 5.4 kPa.
clauses.feedback: A normal number that should frighten you.

cases.resolution: A patient in acute severe asthma is hyperventilating, so the PaCO2 should be low. A normal — let alone raised — PaCO2 means she is tiring and no longer moving enough air to blow off CO2. That reclassifies her from acute severe to life-threatening asthma and makes this an immediate ITU referral for possible ventilation. The lesson generalises: in a patient working hard to breathe, a normal CO2 is not a reassuring result, it is a sign of exhaustion.

clauses.text: A 38-year-old woman presents with widespread bruising and lethargy.
clauses.feedback: The presenting picture of any thrombocytopenia. It does not separate the causes, and the causes are managed very differently.

clauses.text: Her platelet count is 11 x 10^9/L.
clauses.feedback: Severe thrombocytopenia, and it explains the bruising. But the number alone doesn't tell you the mechanism — and in this condition the reflex it invites is the wrong one.

clauses.text: The blood film shows numerous fragmented red cells.
clauses.feedback: Schistocytes change everything.

clauses.text: She has been intermittently confused since yesterday.
clauses.feedback: Right line — fluctuating neurological signs are part of this picture and mark it as urgent. But confusion has many causes in a sick patient; on its own it doesn't establish the mechanism.

clauses.text: Her temperature is 37.9°C.
clauses.feedback: A low-grade fever is common here but is far too non-specific to act on.

cases.resolution: Fragmented red cells mean a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia — with thrombocytopenia and neurological signs, this is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. It is a haematological emergency requiring urgent plasma exchange. Critically, it also makes the instinctive action harmful: platelets must NOT be transfused, because they fuel further microvascular thrombosis. The film is what stops you doing the wrong thing to a platelet count of 11.

clauses.text: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes is admitted with vomiting and abdominal pain.
clauses.feedback: The presentation. It points you towards the diagnosis but not towards the order in which you do things.

clauses.text: Capillary glucose is 29 mmol/L.
clauses.feedback: Part of the diagnostic triad, and it tells you insulin is needed. It does not tell you when to start it.

clauses.text: Blood ketones are 5.2 mmol/L and pH is 7.11.
clauses.feedback: This confirms diabetic ketoacidosis and tells you it is severe. Correct reasoning — but the diagnosis isn't the thing that alters your first move here.

clauses.text: She is drowsy but rousable, with dry mucous membranes.
clauses.feedback: Consistent with the dehydration of DKA. It supports fluid resuscitation, which you were going to do anyway.

clauses.text: Serum potassium is 3.1 mmol/L.
clauses.feedback: This dictates the sequence.

cases.resolution: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly. Starting an insulin infusion in a patient whose potassium is already below 3.5 mmol/L can precipitate life-threatening hypokalaemia and arrhythmia. So this result changes the order of operations: fluids and potassium replacement first, insulin withheld until the potassium is above 3.5. Total body potassium is always depleted in DKA even when the serum level looks normal — a low value at presentation is the alarm.

clauses.text: A 27-year-old woman is brought in after taking paracetamol.
clauses.feedback: The reason for attendance. Everything that matters is in the detail of how and when.

clauses.text: She took the tablets in repeated small handfuls across about fourteen hours.
clauses.feedback: The pattern of ingestion, not the dose, is what decides this.

clauses.text: She estimates a total of around 18 grams.
clauses.feedback: Clearly a significant amount, and it's right to take it seriously. But the total dose isn't what invalidates the nomogram here — the pattern of ingestion does, regardless of how much was actually taken.

clauses.text: Her paracetamol concentration is below the treatment line on the nomogram.
clauses.feedback: Right instinct to check it — but this result is the trap. The nomogram is only valid for a single ingestion at a known time; in a staggered overdose, a level below the line isn't reassuring, it's simply inapplicable. Discharging on the strength of this number is exactly the error the 2012 guidance change exists to prevent.

clauses.text: She feels nauseated but is otherwise well, with normal observations.
clauses.feedback: Early paracetamol toxicity is characteristically silent. Feeling well carries no reassurance at this stage.

cases.resolution: The 2012 MHRA/Commission on Human Medicines revision to the acetylcysteine guidance, implemented via TOXBASE, states that any staggered overdose — tablets not all taken within a single hour — invalidates the treatment nomogram outright, regardless of the total amount ingested. Acetylcysteine is started on the pattern of ingestion alone, not the plotted level. Reading a below-the-line concentration as reassuring here is exactly the error the 2012 change was designed to close off.

clauses.text: A 45-year-old man describes four days of progressive weakness that began in his feet.
clauses.feedback: The ascending pattern is the right thread to pull, and it points at the diagnosis. But the diagnosis is not what determines the next hour.

clauses.text: He had a diarrhoeal illness three weeks ago.
clauses.feedback: Supports the aetiology and is worth documenting, but a historical infection does not change what you do today.

clauses.text: Reflexes are absent throughout and he has a bilateral facial droop.
clauses.feedback: Areflexia with cranial nerve involvement confirms you're dealing with an acute, extensive polyradiculoneuropathy — genuinely severity-defining. But it's a diagnostic and extent marker, not a number with a defined action-threshold. That's what the next finding uniquely supplies.

clauses.text: Forced vital capacity is 1.1 litres, down from 2.0 litres this morning.
clauses.feedback: This is the measurement that moves him.

clauses.text: Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
clauses.feedback: Dangerously reassuring. Saturations stay normal in neuromuscular respiratory failure until the patient is on the edge of arrest — they lag far behind the mechanics.

cases.resolution: In Guillain-Barré syndrome, respiratory failure is neuromuscular, not due to impaired gas exchange, so pulse oximetry stays normal until decompensation is imminent — it lags far behind the mechanics. Serial forced vital capacity is what UK neurology and intensive care practice actually monitors instead: the roughly 20 ml/kg (around 1.5 litres) threshold for escalating to ITU and planning for ventilation traces to Lawn ND et al. (Arch Neurol 2001;58:893), a cohort study now embedded in NHS trust protocols and UK training, rather than a single NICE- or Association of British Neurologists-badged guideline. Exam findings like areflexia and cranial nerve involvement tell you this is severe GBS; FVC is the one measurement with a defined trigger for acting right now.

clauses.text: A 74-year-old woman has had a left-sided headache for three weeks.
clauses.feedback: The presenting symptom. New headache in this age group earns your attention but doesn't set the clock.

clauses.text: Her scalp is tender when she brushes her hair, and her jaw aches when chewing.
clauses.feedback: Strong reasoning — jaw claudication is one of the more specific features of giant cell arteritis and should already have you reaching for steroids. But it isn't what changes the route and the dose.

clauses.text: Yesterday she had twenty minutes of complete visual loss in the left eye, which then resolved.
clauses.feedback: Transient visual loss is the emergency within the emergency.

clauses.text: ESR is 96 mm/hr.
clauses.feedback: Supports the diagnosis and is part of the criteria. But treatment in suspected GCA is never delayed for, or decided by, an inflammatory marker.

clauses.text: Temporal artery biopsy is scheduled for later in the week.
clauses.feedback: Appropriate to arrange, and it stays positive for a week or more after steroids are started — which is exactly why it must never delay treatment.

cases.resolution: Amaurosis fugax in suspected giant cell arteritis signals imminent, irreversible blindness — and once vision is lost in one eye the other typically follows within days. This escalates management from high-dose oral prednisolone to immediate high-dose IV methylprednisolone, given before biopsy and without waiting for the ESR. Visual symptoms are the finding that converts an urgent outpatient problem into a same-hour intervention.

clauses.text: A 58-year-old woman attends with a sore throat and feeling generally run down.
clauses.feedback: On its own, an entirely ordinary presentation you would not act urgently upon.

clauses.text: She completed a cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer ten days ago.
clauses.feedback: This single line rewrites the urgency of everything else.

clauses.text: Her temperature is 38.4°C.
clauses.feedback: Right to notice — fever is the trigger. But in someone with an intact immune system this degree of fever with a sore throat is not a medical emergency. The context is what makes it one.

clauses.text: Chest examination is normal and her chest X-ray is clear.
clauses.feedback: Reassuring-looking and irrelevant to the decision. A neutropenic patient frequently cannot mount the inflammatory response that produces signs or radiographic changes.

clauses.text: Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg and she looks well.
clauses.feedback: Looking well is not protective here, and waiting for haemodynamic compromise before treating is precisely the error this scenario is built to catch.

cases.resolution: Fever within roughly six weeks of chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise — and the nadir around day 7–14 is the highest-risk window. Empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics must be given within one hour, before the neutrophil count returns and regardless of how well the patient looks or how normal the examination is. These patients deteriorate precipitously and without warning.

clauses.text: A 71-year-old man with chronic kidney disease attends feeling weak and lethargic.
clauses.feedback: Non-specific, and typical of the condition at any severity.

clauses.text: He was started on ramipril and spironolactone six weeks ago.
clauses.feedback: Good reasoning — this identifies the likely cause and tells you what to stop. But causation doesn't determine what you give in the next five minutes.

clauses.text: The ECG shows a broad, bizarre QRS complex approaching a sine wave.
clauses.feedback: The ECG, not the number, decides the first drug.

clauses.text: Serum potassium is 6.3 mmol/L.
clauses.feedback: Elevated, and it demands treatment. But at this level it's a monitoring and escalation threshold, not an automatic calcium trigger — the same potassium with a normal ECG calls for a different first step.

clauses.text: Creatinine is 280 µmol/L, similar to his baseline.
clauses.feedback: An unchanged creatinine tells you this is his usual renal function, not an acute injury. It doesn't alter the emergency in front of you.

cases.resolution: Broad QRS complexes and sine-wave morphology mean the hyperkalaemia is already destabilising the myocardium, and cardiac arrest may be minutes away. Per the UK Kidney Association's October 2023 hyperkalaemia guideline and Resuscitation Council UK, IV calcium is triggered by these ECG changes specifically — not by crossing a particular potassium number, which the guideline instead uses as the threshold for escalated monitoring (K+ ≥6.5 mmol/L defines severe hyperkalaemia). That mandates IV calcium gluconate immediately to stabilise the membrane — before insulin-dextrose, before salbutamol, and before anything that lowers the potassium, none of which protect the heart quickly enough. Treat the ECG, not the laboratory value.

clauses.text: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension has severe chest pain.
clauses.feedback: Hypertension is a risk factor for several things at once here. It doesn't discriminate between them.

clauses.text: The pain was maximal at onset and tears through to between his shoulder blades.
clauses.feedback: Strong reasoning — instantaneous, tearing, interscapular pain is a classic presentation of acute aortic syndrome. But history alone doesn't stop the ACS pathway being activated; an objective sign is what the diagnostic split actually turns on.

clauses.text: Blood pressure is 178/96 mmHg in the right arm and 142/84 mmHg in the left.
clauses.feedback: An interarm differential is the objective sign that changes the pathway.

clauses.text: The ECG shows minor ST depression in the lateral leads.
clauses.feedback: This is the trap, not the answer. Non-specific ECG changes invite you to treat this as an acute coronary syndrome — which is the dangerous move.

clauses.text: He has been given aspirin, and thrombolysis is being arranged.
clauses.feedback: The default reflex for chest pain with ECG changes — and exactly what should wait until dissection is excluded. Antiplatelets and thrombolysis can be catastrophic if this is dissection, not a coronary event.

cases.resolution: Per the ESC 2014 Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Aortic Diseases, a significant interarm blood pressure difference (typically ≥20 mmHg) raises suspicion of acute aortic syndrome and should prompt urgent CT aortography — with ACS treatment (antiplatelets, anticoagulation, thrombolysis) withheld until dissection is excluded, since these can be catastrophic if the true diagnosis is dissection compromising flow to one subclavian artery. Management becomes urgent imaging with aggressive blood pressure and heart rate control instead. Always check both arms before treating chest pain as ACS — and before continuing treatment already started on that assumption.

clauses.text: A 51-year-old man presents having vomited a large volume of fresh blood.
clauses.feedback: This establishes a significant upper gastrointestinal bleed and drives resuscitation. But the resuscitation is the same whatever the source — something else changes the drugs.

clauses.text: Pulse is 118 bpm with a blood pressure of 96/58 mmHg.
clauses.feedback: Right to register the haemodynamic compromise; it sets the urgency and the transfusion threshold. It does not tell you the cause.

clauses.text: He takes ibuprofen most days for back pain.
clauses.feedback: A deliberate distractor. NSAIDs are a genuine cause of peptic ulceration, and following that thread leads you away from the finding that matters more.

clauses.text: He has spider naevi, palmar erythema and shifting dullness.
clauses.feedback: The signs of chronic liver disease change the treatment, not just the diagnosis.

clauses.text: His haemoglobin is 78 g/L.
clauses.feedback: Guides transfusion, and worth acting on. But the number is the consequence of the bleed rather than a clue to its origin.

cases.resolution: Stigmata of chronic liver disease with portal hypertension mean this is a variceal bleed until proven otherwise, and that adds two specific interventions to standard resuscitation: terlipressin to reduce portal pressure, and prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics, which independently reduce mortality in cirrhotic gastrointestinal bleeding. Endoscopy becomes band ligation rather than ulcer therapy. Missing the liver signs means missing both drugs.

clauses.text: A 44-year-old woman attends with a severe headache and vomiting.
clauses.feedback: Common and undifferentiated. Almost every headache presentation looks like this at the door.

clauses.text: The headache reached its worst intensity within a couple of seconds of starting.
clauses.feedback: The speed of onset, not the severity, is the discriminator.

clauses.text: She has a long history of migraine and says this feels like a bad one.
clauses.feedback: The anchoring trap. A previous headache diagnosis is one of the commonest reasons this condition is missed, and the patient's own comparison is not a safe filter.

clauses.text: She has mild neck stiffness and dislikes the light.
clauses.feedback: Right direction — meningism supports the concern and warrants investigation. But it appears late, is often absent early, and is shared with meningitis.

clauses.text: Neurological examination is otherwise entirely normal.
clauses.feedback: Offers no reassurance whatsoever. Most patients with this diagnosis have a normal neurological examination at presentation.

cases.resolution: Thunderclap headache — maximal within seconds — is subarachnoid haemorrhage until excluded, irrespective of a migraine history or a normal examination. It mandates immediate non-contrast CT head; if that is negative and presentation is beyond six hours, lumbar puncture at twelve hours looking for xanthochromia. The character of the onset is doing all the diagnostic work here, which is why the history must be taken precisely: not 'how bad' but 'how fast'.

clauses.text: A 29-year-old woman with known Addison's disease, normally well-controlled on maintenance hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for two days.
clauses.feedback: Known diagnosis, already on treatment, and exactly the kind of minor illness sick-day rules exist for — the puzzle here isn't what's wrong, it's what's different about today.

clauses.text: She has not been able to keep her regular hydrocortisone tablets down for the last two days.
clauses.feedback: This is what turns 'take more tablets' into 'give the injection.'

clauses.text: She looks dehydrated, with a pulse of 118 bpm and blood pressure of 88/54 mmHg.
clauses.feedback: Real evidence of volume depletion, and it correctly raises urgency. But this is exactly the kind of picture her normal sick-day dose is meant to cover — it doesn't yet tell you why today needs more than that.

clauses.text: Sodium is 128 mmol/L and potassium is 5.8 mmol/L.
clauses.feedback: The pattern fits mineralocorticoid deficiency and supports how unwell she is. But she runs this tendency at baseline when unwell — it doesn't by itself change the sick-day plan she already has.

clauses.text: The plan is to double her oral hydrocortisone dose, as she was advised to do the last time she was unwell.
clauses.feedback: Doubling the oral dose is genuinely correct sick-day advice — for a patient who can keep tablets down. It's the wrong instruction for someone who's just told you she can't.

cases.resolution: Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance (2020) sets out "sick day rules" for known adrenal insufficiency: minor intercurrent illness is managed by doubling the oral hydrocortisone dose. That advice assumes the tablets stay down. Vomiting, or any inability to take or absorb oral medication, converts the same illness into an indication for an emergency 100 mg IM or IV hydrocortisone injection and same-day hospital admission, regardless of how the observations look at that exact moment. Increasing a dose she cannot absorb treats nothing — the injection is what the guidance actually calls for here.

clauses.text: A tall, slim 22-year-old man develops sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness.
clauses.feedback: The classic demographic and history for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax — which is managed quite differently from what is developing here.

clauses.text: There is no air entry on the right with hyper-resonant percussion.
clauses.feedback: Correct reasoning, and it confirms a pneumothorax. But a simple pneumothorax of any size still allows time for a chest X-ray first.

clauses.text: Respiratory rate is 34 and saturations are 89% on high-flow oxygen.
clauses.feedback: Marks severe respiratory compromise and demands escalated management. But per BTS's own high-risk criteria, significant hypoxia is managed on the standard imaging pathway (X-ray, then aspiration or drain) — it's tension physiology specifically, not hypoxia severity, that skips imaging.

clauses.text: A chest X-ray has been requested and the porter is on the way.
clauses.feedback: Reasonable in most pneumothoraces — and exactly the delay that kills in this one. Watch what the other findings do to the appropriateness of waiting.

clauses.text: The trachea is deviated to the left, blood pressure is 78/44 mmHg and the JVP is raised.
clauses.feedback: Tracheal deviation with haemodynamic collapse removes the imaging step entirely.

cases.resolution: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side with hypotension and a raised JVP is a tension pneumothorax: intrathoracic pressure is obstructing venous return, and this is obstructive shock. Per the BTS Pleural Disease Guideline 2023, this is treated as a clinical diagnosis — immediate needle decompression followed by a chest drain, with no chest X-ray beforehand — while significant hypoxia and other high-risk features are managed on the standard imaging-led pathway. Sending this patient to radiology is the classic fatal error; a simple or even severely hypoxic pneumothorax can wait for a film, a tension pneumothorax cannot.

clauses.text: A 54-year-old man reports three months of fatigue, weight loss and drenching night sweats.
clauses.feedback: B symptoms. They tell you something chronic is going on, over a timescale of months rather than hours.

clauses.text: He has massive splenomegaly crossing the midline.
clauses.feedback: Right direction — this narrows you towards a myeloproliferative disorder. But splenomegaly has been developing for months and does not dictate today's intervention.

clauses.text: White cell count is 310 x 10^9/L with a full spectrum of granulocyte precursors.
clauses.feedback: Very close, and this degree of leucocytosis should worry you. A high count alone, though, is treated with cytoreduction on a scale of days — something here makes it an emergency.

clauses.text: The leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score is low.
clauses.feedback: Diagnostically useful — a low score distinguishes chronic myeloid leukaemia from a reactive leukaemoid reaction, where it would be raised. But being diagnostically important is not the same as being management-changing, and this is largely a historical test now superseded by BCR-ABL testing.

clauses.text: He has had a painful, sustained erection since the early hours of this morning.
clauses.feedback: Priapism here is not a urological problem — it is a rheology emergency.

cases.resolution: Priapism with a white cell count this high is leukostasis: the blood is too viscous to perfuse the microcirculation, and the same process threatens the cerebral and pulmonary beds. It converts a chronic leukaemia into a same-day emergency requiring urgent leukapheresis and cytoreduction. Note the discrimination being trained here — the LAP score is the most diagnostically interesting finding in the stem, and the priapism is the one that changes what you do in the next hour. They are not the same thing.

clauses.text: An 80-year-old woman has felt dizzy on standing for the past week.
clauses.feedback: A week of symptoms establishes chronicity, which argues against — not for — immediate intervention.

clauses.text: Her ECG shows complete dissociation of P waves and QRS complexes at a rate of 34.
clauses.feedback: Correct identification of complete heart block, and it certainly means she needs a permanent pacemaker eventually. But per the Resuscitation Council UK bradycardia algorithm, the rhythm diagnosis itself never dictates timing — adverse features do.

clauses.text: She takes bisoprolol for hypertension.
clauses.feedback: Worth spotting and worth stopping, since it may be contributing. A drug history explains a cause to remove, not a timing decision — the algorithm's adverse-features check is what actually decides urgency.

clauses.text: Blood pressure is 74/40 mmHg and she is drowsy and confused.
clauses.feedback: Adverse features, not the rhythm, decide the timing.

clauses.text: Her GP has been asked to arrange a routine outpatient pacing referral.
clauses.feedback: The right endpoint — she does need a pacemaker — reached by the wrong route. Adverse features make this today's emergency, not next month's outpatient list.

cases.resolution: Per the Resuscitation Council UK bradycardia algorithm, the decision to intervene immediately turns on adverse features — shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or heart failure — not on the heart rate or the rhythm label itself. Hypotension with reduced consciousness makes this an emergency requiring atropine and immediate transcutaneous or transvenous pacing, rather than a routine outpatient referral for an urgent-but-planned permanent pacemaker. The same ECG in a well, normotensive patient is a very different problem.

clauses.text: A 19-year-old university student has had fever and headache since last night, and his GP has been called out for an out-of-hours home visit.
clauses.feedback: The reason for the visit — it tells you to take this seriously, not what to do before the ambulance arrives.

clauses.text: He has photophobia and marked neck stiffness.
clauses.feedback: Right line — meningism raises real concern and justifies urgent transfer. But on its own it's still "call an ambulance and get him to hospital," not "treat him here first."

clauses.text: There is a purpuric rash over his trunk that does not blanch under a glass.
clauses.feedback: This is the finding that changes what you do right now, in his living room.

clauses.text: He is drowsy and takes longer than usual to answer questions.
clauses.feedback: A genuine severity marker, and it should worry you. It still only argues for how fast the ambulance needs to be — not for what you do with your bag before it arrives.

clauses.text: An ambulance has been called, and the plan is to give antibiotics once he arrives at hospital.
clauses.feedback: Correct instinct to call an ambulance — wrong to wait for it. Giving the injection now doesn't delay the transfer; withholding it does delay the treatment.

cases.resolution: Per NICE NG240 (2024), suspected bacterial meningitis without a rash is treated urgently in hospital — antibiotics within around an hour of arrival — but pre-hospital antibiotics are only advised if transfer would otherwise be significantly delayed. A non-blanching rash changes that threshold: NG240 recommends giving IM or IV benzylpenicillin (or a third-generation cephalosporin) as soon as possible in the community, provided it doesn't delay transfer to hospital. The rash doesn't make hospital treatment more urgent — timing there is similar either way — it specifically licenses treating before the ambulance even arrives, in the one setting where every minute is entirely in your hands.

clauses.text: A 41-year-old woman with Graves' disease attends three days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
clauses.feedback: Good reasoning — recent surgery is a recognised precipitant in a patient with known thyrotoxicosis. It raises your index of suspicion without confirming anything.

clauses.text: She has a fine tremor and a smooth goitre.
clauses.feedback: The signs of her underlying, chronic thyrotoxicosis. They were present before this admission.

clauses.text: She is in atrial fibrillation at 148 bpm.
clauses.feedback: Close. Tachyarrhythmia is part of the picture and needs treating, but atrial fibrillation alone is common in ordinary thyrotoxicosis and doesn't meet Burch-Wartofsky/ATA criteria for storm by itself — it doesn't signal decompensation on its own.

clauses.text: Her temperature is 39.9°C and she is agitated and disorientated.
clauses.feedback: Fever with altered mental state is what converts thyrotoxicosis into a storm.

clauses.text: TSH is undetectable with a free T4 of 41 pmol/L.
clauses.feedback: Confirms thyrotoxicosis but does not grade it. Hormone levels in thyroid storm overlap almost completely with uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis — the diagnosis is clinical.

cases.resolution: Thyroid storm is diagnosed clinically, not biochemically: hyperpyrexia and central nervous system dysfunction — agitation, delirium, or coma — in a thyrotoxic patient, usually with a precipitant such as surgery or infection. UK practice imports this from the American Thyroid Association/AACE 2016 hyperthyroidism guideline (Ross DS et al., Thyroid 2016) and commonly uses the Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale as a bedside aid — there is no dedicated NICE or British Thyroid Association document specifically on thyroid storm. Mortality is substantial and treatment must not wait for thyroid function tests. It requires immediate combined therapy: beta-blockade, propylthiouracil, iodine given at least an hour after the thionamide, corticosteroids, and active cooling.

clauses.text: A 66-year-old woman develops urticaria and facial swelling minutes after a first dose of intravenous antibiotic.
clauses.feedback: This establishes anaphylaxis and tells you to give intramuscular adrenaline immediately. Correct — but the question is what to do when that doesn't work.

clauses.text: She has audible stridor and is wheezing throughout.
clauses.feedback: Airway and breathing compromise confirming severity. It reinforces the need for adrenaline rather than changing the drug.

clauses.text: Blood pressure is 68/38 mmHg.
clauses.feedback: Circulatory collapse, and part of the same picture. It tells you she is peri-arrest but not why she isn't responding.

clauses.text: She remains hypotensive and stridulous after three doses of intramuscular adrenaline and two litres of fluid.
clauses.feedback: Very close — recognising refractoriness is the right step and should prompt you to ask why. Now find the reason in the stem.

clauses.text: Her regular medications include bisoprolol, which she took this morning.
clauses.feedback: Beta-blockade explains the failure and points at a specific antidote.

cases.resolution: Beta-blockers blunt the response to adrenaline, producing anaphylaxis that is refractory to standard treatment. The specific answer is intravenous glucagon, which increases cardiac inotropy and chronotropy through a receptor pathway that bypasses the blocked beta-adrenoceptor entirely. Without this, escalating adrenaline doses achieve little. The drug history is the finding that explains an otherwise inexplicable failure to respond.

clauses.text: A 46-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder is brought in confused and unsteady.
clauses.feedback: The presentation. Confusion and ataxia in a psychiatric patient have a wide differential, including several drug effects.

clauses.text: She has a coarse tremor, ataxia and brisk reflexes with intermittent myoclonic jerks.
clauses.feedback: Strong reasoning — this neurological signature is characteristic of the toxicity in question and tells you what is happening. But it doesn't tell you why it happened now, after years of stability.

clauses.text: She has taken the same dose of lithium for eight years with stable levels.
clauses.feedback: An important observation, and it should make you ask what changed. Stable dosing means the cause lies outside the prescription itself.

clauses.text: Her GP added ramipril and bendroflumethiazide for hypertension three weeks ago.
clauses.feedback: The new drugs are the mechanism and the thing you must stop.

clauses.text: She has been vomiting for two days.
clauses.feedback: Right thread, and a strong one — volume depletion is itself a BNF-recognised aggravating factor for lithium retention, not just a symptom of it. It's tempting to stop here and call this dehydration. But eight years of stability makes 'just vomiting' an incomplete explanation on its own — something still needs to explain why her kidneys are suddenly retaining lithium in the first place.

cases.resolution: Lithium is renally excreted and its clearance falls with anything that reduces renal perfusion or increases sodium reabsorption. Per the BNF's interaction data, ACE inhibitors, thiazide diuretics and NSAIDs all raise lithium levels and are classic precipitants of toxicity in a patient stable for years. Management is to stop the offending drugs and the lithium, rehydrate with saline, and consider haemodialysis in severe toxicity. The drug history, not the neurology or the vomiting alone, is where the answer lives.

clauses.text: A 54-year-old man attended his GP three days ago with exertional chest pain, which settled with rest and has not recurred since.
clauses.feedback: The story of a chest pain that already settled tells you he survived it — it doesn't tell you whether the vessel behind it is still critical.

clauses.text: He is a current smoker with type 2 diabetes and a strong family history of ischaemic heart disease.
clauses.feedback: Real risk factors, and they should raise your index of suspicion. But risk factors alone don't diagnose critical stenosis — plenty of patients with this exact profile have unremarkable coronary arteries.

clauses.text: He is entirely pain-free now, and his cardiac troponin is normal.
clauses.feedback: Feeling well with a normal troponin is exactly the trap. This ECG pattern is classically seen between episodes of ischaemia — the patient is often asymptomatic and biomarker-negative when it's recorded.

clauses.text: His ECG shows deep, symmetrical T-wave inversion in leads V2 and V3.
clauses.feedback: This is the pattern that changes everything.

clauses.text: An outpatient exercise tolerance test has been booked for next week to further assess his chest pain.
clauses.feedback: This is the dangerous instinct, not the safe one. Provoking ischaemia in a vessel this critical can trigger a large anterior infarction on the treadmill.

cases.resolution: Deep, symmetrical T-wave inversion in V2-3 in a patient who has just had unstable angina is Wellens' syndrome — an ECG marker of critical stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery, seen precisely because the patient is currently pain-free and the vessel has not yet occluded. It carries a high risk of extensive anterior myocardial infarction if left untreated, so it mandates prompt coronary angiography rather than an outpatient wait-and-see approach. Provocative testing — exercise ECG or pharmacological stress imaging — is contraindicated: it can precipitate the very infarction the pattern is warning you about. A normal troponin and a settled story are not, on their own, reassuring once the ECG carries this pattern.

clauses.text: A 61-year-old man had a drug-eluting stent placed in his right coronary artery seventeen days ago, after presenting with an NSTEMI.
clauses.feedback: Establishes the anatomy and the timeline — useful context, but a stent seventeen days old doesn't itself tell you whether today's pain is routine or a new occlusion.

clauses.text: He describes central chest tightness that feels identical to the angina he had before his stent.
clauses.feedback: Right instinct — pain that matches his known angina says this is almost certainly cardiac. It doesn't yet tell you whether this is the same disease behaving as before, or something new happening inside the stent.

clauses.text: He ran out of his clopidogrel five days ago and has not taken any since.
clauses.feedback: This explains a mechanism and should worry you — per ESC/EACTS guidance, premature discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy is the classic precipitant of stent thrombosis. But stent thrombosis occurs even with perfect adherence; this raises suspicion, it isn't required for the diagnosis and doesn't confirm the event is happening right now.

clauses.text: The pain has not eased despite three sprays of sublingual GTN.
clauses.feedback: This is what separates today from every other episode he's had.

clauses.text: The plan is to increase his isosorbide mononitrate dose and review him in clinic next week.
clauses.feedback: The right move for genuinely worsening stable angina — and the wrong one here. Pain like this after a stent needs emergency reassessment now, not anti-anginal escalation on an outpatient timeline.

cases.resolution: Per the 2018 ESC/EACTS Guidelines on Myocardial Revascularization (§13.4.3), angina that reproduces a patient's usual pain but fails to respond to sublingual nitrates, in the weeks after stent placement, is stent thrombosis until proven otherwise — a near-complete or complete re-occlusion of the treated vessel, most classically precipitated by early cessation of dual antiplatelet therapy, though it can occur even with perfect adherence. Because the occlusion is typically more complete than the original lesion, it behaves like a fresh STEMI: this is a medical emergency requiring immediate reassessment, urgent ECG and troponin, and prompt reactivation of the primary PCI pathway — not another dose of GTN, and not an outpatient medication review. Nitrate-refractoriness is the finding that tells you the story has changed, even when the pain sounds exactly like it always has.

clauses.text: A 68-year-old woman is recovering on the coronary care unit, four days after a large anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
clauses.feedback: Sets the scene and the timing. Day four after a large infarct is exactly the window this complication occurs in — but the day alone doesn't tell you what's gone wrong.

clauses.text: She has become acutely breathless over the last hour, with a respiratory rate of 32 and oxygen saturations of 88% on high-flow oxygen.
clauses.feedback: Real and worrying — acute hypoxic breathlessness this soon after a big infarct should make you think about a new mechanical problem, not just 'more heart failure.' It doesn't yet tell you which one.

clauses.text: Blood pressure has fallen to 82/54 mmHg.
clauses.feedback: Cardiogenic shock is now on the table, and it demands urgent senior review. But hypotension alone is shared by several post-infarct catastrophes — pump failure, free wall rupture, reinfarction — so it doesn't discriminate between them.

clauses.text: A new pansystolic murmur, loudest at the apex, has appeared since this morning.
clauses.feedback: A new murmur days after an MI is never just an incidental finding.

clauses.text: She has been started on IV furosemide and referred to the heart failure team.
clauses.feedback: Reasonable first instinct for post-MI pulmonary oedema — and exactly the wrong fix here. Diuretics and vasodilators won't correct a flail mitral leaflet; this needs a surgeon, not a heart-failure round.

cases.resolution: Per ESC 2023 ACS guidance and the 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease, a new pansystolic murmur loudest at the apex, days after a myocardial infarction, with acute pulmonary oedema and hypotension, is papillary muscle rupture causing acute severe mitral regurgitation until proven otherwise. It typically occurs within the first week post-infarction, most classically with inferior or posterior infarcts affecting the posteromedial papillary muscle, which — unlike the dual-supplied anterolateral muscle — relies on a single blood supply. Unlike routine post-MI heart failure, this is a surgical emergency: standard diuretic and vasodilator therapy will not fix a flail mitral leaflet, and the patient needs urgent echocardiography and inotropic or mechanical support to bridge to emergency mitral valve repair or replacement. The murmur, not the breathlessness or the blood pressure, is what tells you which emergency you are in.

clauses.text: A 38-year-old woman describes several episodes of central chest tightness over the past month, always occurring between 3 and 5 a.m. while she is asleep.
clauses.feedback: The circadian pattern — pain clustering in the small hours — is a genuine clue, but on its own it's just an unusual story, not a diagnosis.

clauses.text: Each episode settles rapidly with sublingual GTN.
clauses.feedback: Rapid relief with GTN is consistent with a vasospastic or ischaemic process either way; it narrows the field without settling the question of what's actually obstructing flow — or whether anything is.

clauses.text: An ECG recorded during one episode showed transient ST elevation that had completely resolved half an hour later, with no rise in troponin.
clauses.feedback: Transient ST elevation that fully resolves, with no troponin rise, is exactly the pattern of vasospastic angina. Strong reasoning — but a fixed, high-grade stenosis with intermittent plaque instability can look similar on the surface.

clauses.text: Coronary angiography, performed while she was symptomatic, shows no significant stenosis anywhere in her coronary arteries.
clauses.feedback: A normal angiogram during an actual episode is what rules out fixed disease and rules in vasospasm.

clauses.text: She smokes ten cigarettes a day and has a family history of ischaemic heart disease.
clauses.feedback: Real risk factors for atherosclerosis, and easy to anchor on. But they describe her risk of one disease while the angiogram in front of you is telling you she doesn't have it — at least not the obstructive kind.

cases.resolution: Chest pain at rest, characteristically clustering in the early hours, with transient ST elevation that resolves spontaneously and a coronary angiogram free of significant stenosis, is Prinzmetal's (variant) angina — coronary artery vasospasm rather than fixed atherosclerotic obstruction. This changes the pharmacology: first-line treatment is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine or nifedipine to relax the vessel wall, with long-acting nitrates as an add-on. Beta-blockers, the default second agent in ordinary stable angina, are avoided here — unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction can worsen the spasm they're meant to treat. Smoking history and family history describe her risk of atherosclerosis; the angiogram is what tells you which disease she actually has.
